name: Self storage business
blurb: Rent out storage units to households and businesses, usually month to month
title: Self Storage Business: How Storage Units Make Money
description: How a self storage or storage unit business makes money, the land, permits and insurance it needs, who it suits, the risks and how to test local demand.
h1: How to start a self storage business
answer: A self storage business rents units of different sizes to households and businesses, usually month to month, and earns rent once units are filled. It is a property business: land or a building, construction or conversion, and financing are the main costs, and the risk is that units fill more slowly than your loan payments are due.

sections.h: How a storage unit business makes money
body: Tenants pay rent per unit, priced by size and features such as climate control or drive-up access. Extra income comes from locks, boxes, packing supplies, tenant insurance and sometimes vehicle or boat parking.

Costs include the mortgage or lease, property tax, insurance, security systems, maintenance, management software, marketing and any staff. Because rent arrives unit by unit, the slow months while a new site fills are the hardest to fund.

ul: Land or a building with zoning that allows storage use; converting an empty building is one common route.
Construction or conversion: units, doors, lighting, gates and access control.
Security: cameras, alarms and electronic gate access are what tenants look for.
Rental contracts that follow your local storage and lien laws, including what happens when a tenant stops paying. Rules differ by country and state; get legal advice.
Property and liability insurance, management software and a way for people to find and book units online.

sections.h: Who it suits (and who it doesn't)

head: Suits
Not for
rows: Property investors with capital or financing
People without access to land, savings or credit
Owners comfortable with permits, builders and loans
People who like steady admin and customer service
Areas already full of storage with discounting

ul: Oversupply: new facilities nearby can force price cuts.
Lease-up time: a new site may take a long time to fill while costs run from day one.
Defaulting tenants: in the US, operators can hold lien sales under each jurisdiction's law, but only after required notices; get the process wrong and you face legal claims.
Buying an existing facility: check occupancy, rent rolls and bank records yourself, not just the seller's figures.
Franchise, course or "turnkey" development pitches; read every fee and earnings claim carefully.

sections.h: How to test it cheaply first

ol: Map storage facilities within a short drive of your target area.
Call or check their sites for available sizes and prices, and whether they offer move-in discounts.
Ask the local planning office whether storage use is allowed on a candidate site.
Get rough quotes for conversion or construction and financing terms.
Model how many units must be rented to cover loan payments and running costs; stop if that occupancy looks out of reach.
Confirm zoning and permits before committing to land or a lease.
Have a lawyer draft rental agreements that follow local lien rules.
Set up gates, cameras, insurance and management software.
Get the site listed on maps and storage search sites before opening.
Track occupancy, rent collected and late payments weekly.

faq.a: Less work than many businesses once it is full, but not passive. Tenants need help, units need cleaning and repairs, and late payers need following up under legal rules.

faq.q: Can I start small with storage containers?
faq.a: Some owners start with shipping containers on land they control, but zoning, permits and security still apply. Check local rules before placing any.

faq.q: What happens when a tenant stops paying?
faq.a: It depends on local law. In many US states, operators can sell the contents after giving formal notice, and the tenant can stop the sale by paying in full. Get legal advice before you write your contracts.
